output.brief: The evidence points mainly at Callerby, not Halden. The platform's tamper-proof audit trail shows the architect answered 62 of 64 RFIs within the contract period (median 4 working days). The two late ones were on finishes, and Callerby itself marked them as having no programme impact. Of the 41 RFIs the draft claim calls late, 39 sat in Callerby's own draft status for 9–47 days before they were submitted. The claim's late-information argument therefore fails. The tower crane went to Kestrel in October 2025 and came back in April. The daily diaries say 'frame on hold – design' every day while steel sat on the ground, and level 3 steel started right after the crane returned. That fits a Callerby redeployment decision, though I haven't proved it. Halden's change orders, especially CO-09, may have contributed, but we have not checked them, so their share is unknown. Don't submit the claim as drafted: it overstates the case and risks credibility. Don't punish the superintendent, who told the truth. Don't suspend the incentive scheme yet, because the link to the crane move is unproven. Next steps: get the change order register and crane ledger checked, then have an independent analyst decide whether a reduced claim is defensible. Also review Fenmore's contingency fee and how Gareth signed off the diaries.
